readerTitle: Why a quick yes from your team can be a warning sign
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Janis의 집단사고 이론과 후속 연구 리뷰) + 가상 사례 (배관 회사, 원예용품점, 소프트웨어 스타트업)
insight: 팀의 만장일치는 반대하기가 안전했을 때만 의미가 있다. 동의의 속도보다 반대 의견이 나올 기회가 있었는지를 본다.
misconception: 가까운 팀이 빠르게 모두 동의했다면 좋은 결정이라는 신호다.

sources.text: Janis, I. L. (1972). Victims of Groupthink. Houghton Mifflin.
Janis, I. L. (1982). Groupthink: Psychological Studies of Policy Decisions and Fiascoes (2nd ed.). Houghton Mifflin.
Esser, J. K. (1998). Alive and well after 25 years: A review of groupthink research. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 73(2–3), 116–141.
배관 회사, 원예용품점, 소프트웨어 스타트업 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "groupthink"라는 단어는 William H. Whyte가 1952년에 먼저 썼고, Janis가 1972년에 이론으로 발전시켰습니다. 카드에는 "developed the idea"로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 연도와 서지 정보를 다시 확인하세요.
5번 카드의 징후 목록은 Janis의 8가지 증상 중 일부를 쉬운 말로 줄인 것입니다(만장일치의 착각, 자기 검열, 반대자에 대한 압력, 경고 합리화). 원문 표현과 대조하세요.
6번 카드의 대응책(리더가 먼저 의견을 밝히지 않기, 악마의 대변인, 외부 전문가, 두 번째 기회 회의)은 Janis(1982)가 제안한 처방에 근거합니다. 원문 대조 필요.
"후속 연구는 Janis 모델 전체에 대해 엇갈린 지지를 보였다"는 Esser(1998) 리뷰의 결론을 일반적으로 요약한 것입니다. 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
모든 사업 사례와 수치(6명, 10분, 아파트 40채 등)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Six people agreed in ten minutes. That was the problem.
body: At a plumbing company's Monday meeting, the owner pitched a big new contract. Six heads nodded. The decision was made before the coffee cooled.
Across town, a garden-supply store spent an hour arguing about a second location, then decided to wait. Only one of these teams made a costly mistake.

image.label: A meeting where everyone nods, next to a meeting with raised hands
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 3D 클레이 일러스트. 왼쪽: 작업복 차림 여섯 명이 테이블에 앉아 똑같이 고개를 끄덕이고, 한 명은 입술을 꾹 다물고 있음. 오른쪽: 원예용품점 직원 다섯 명이 메모지를 들고 서로 다른 방향을 가리키며 토론. 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Whose yes would you trust more?
body: The plumbing team of six has worked together for twelve years. They agreed to the contract in ten minutes. Nobody raised a concern.
At the garden store, four of five people backed the plan after an hour. They had also written a list of risks along the way.

options.text: The plumbers'. A close team that agrees fast knows its business
options.feedback: Experience counts. But fast, total agreement can also mean nobody felt free to object, and you can't tell which from the vote alone.

options.text: The garden store's. Its yes survived real objections
options.feedback: A yes that came after doubts were voiced tells you the plan was actually tested. It costs an hour, but the hour bought information.

options.text: Neither. Only the results will tell
options.feedback: Results do settle it eventually. But you have to decide before the results arrive, so how the decision was made is the evidence you have.

cards.title: The doubts were there. Nobody said them.
body: The plumbing contract covered 40 new apartments for a developer. It tied up the crew for months. Regular customers waited weeks for repairs, and some never came back.
Later, three of the six admitted they'd doubted the timeline from the start. Why stay quiet? *"The boss was excited." "Nobody else objected."*

At the garden store, the owner asked everyone to write down concerns before she shared her own view. A cashier pointed out that the new site had no space for bulk soil deliveries. They waited and found a better site.

image.label: Thought bubbles with doubts above silent team members
image.brief: 배관 회사 회의 장면. 여섯 명 중 세 명의 머리 위에 작은 생각 풍선("Too many jobs?", "Our regulars?", "Timeline?")이 떠 있지만 입은 닫혀 있음. 테이블 위에는 서명된 계약서. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Groupthink
body: **Groupthink** happens when a group's wish to agree becomes stronger than its wish to get the decision right. People hold back doubts to keep the peace, and the silence looks like support.
Psychologist Irving Janis developed the idea in 1972. His key point: it hits *close-knit* teams hardest. The more people like and trust each other, the more it can feel disloyal to object.

cards.title: The warning signs
body: Janis described signs that a group is drifting into groupthink. Several showed up in the plumbing meeting.
list: **Silence read as agreement:** nobody objects, so everyone assumes everyone agrees
**Self-censorship:** people drop doubts before saying them
**Pressure on the odd one out:** a single objector is told to be a team player
**Explaining warnings away:** bad news gets a quick reason why it doesn't apply
cards.callout: The danger isn't conflict. It's the conflict that never gets said out loud.

cards.title: Make disagreeing cheap.
body: Janis suggested a few habits. The leader shares a view **last**, not first. People write their concerns down before discussion. Someone is asked to argue the other side. For big calls, an outsider reviews the plan, and the group meets once more before committing.
The garden store used the first two. Neither one cost much more than an hour.
cards.softwareNote: Remote teams have their own version: in a video call, cameras off and no one unmuting looks like agreement. A short written poll before the call, where each person names one risk, does the same job as the garden store's notes.

cards.title: Not every agreement is groupthink.
body: Sometimes the answer is just obvious, and a close team that acts quickly is an advantage. Later research found mixed support for Janis's full model, so treat the signs as warnings, not a diagnosis.
The fixes cost time, and they can turn into theater. A devil's advocate everyone knows is just playing a role is easy to ignore. Save the full process for big decisions that are hard to reverse.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: You lead a seven-person software startup. In the planning call, you propose dropping the free plan. Two people say "makes sense." The rest stay quiet. You want a decision by Friday.

options.text: Take the silence as a yes and announce the change
options.feedback: Fast and clean, but you're counting quiet as support. If the doubters were right, you'll hear about it from churned users instead of your team.

options.text: Ask each person to message you privately with the strongest reason not to do it
options.feedback: It costs a day, and you get the objections without the social pressure of the call. You can still decide by Friday.

options.text: Ask the group, "Does anyone disagree?" and wait
options.feedback: Better than nothing. But you've already said what you want, in front of everyone, so the same pressure that kept people quiet is still in the room.

cards.title: A yes is only worth something if saying no was safe.
body: When a team agrees fast, ask whether anyone had a real chance to disagree.
**Try it today:** at your next decision meeting, ask everyone to write down one risk before you share your own view.
